How to transfer assets with the Cell Model is a surprisingly complex subject because of the state rent requirements. We wanted to share a guide on seven patterns (both current and future) that developers should understand.

Design Patterns: UTXO Transfers Using the Cell Model

This document explores different patterns for transferring digital assets between two parties using the Nervos CKB Cell Model. While focused on the CKB blockchain, these patterns may also apply to other UTXO blockchains that implement state rent.

State rent is essential because it ensures sustainable network economics and prevents out of control cost spirals. However, it introduces unique challenges that require innovative design patterns to maintain usability.

Some of the transfer patterns mentioned in this document are tied directly to specific asset protocols. This document aims to focus specifically on the transfer patterns introduced, not the details of the asset protocols themselves.

Challenges of State Rent

State rent presents unique obstacles for UTXO-based token transfers that don’t exist in traditional blockchain models. Understanding these challenges is essential for designing effective transfer patterns.

CKB implements state rent through a simple economic model: 1 CKB token equals 1 byte of permanent on-chain storage capacity. When you create a cell containing smart contracts, assets such as tokens and NFTs, or any other data, the cell’s capacity must cover the storage cost of all these components. This capacity remains locked the entire time the asset exists on-chain. When the assets are destroyed and the cell is consumed, the locked CKB is returned.

The amount of CKB that must be locked depends on the amount of required on-chain data, which can vary from asset to asset. For the most basic asset, the CKB native token, the cost is 61 CKB. For an SUDT token, the cost is 142 CKB. For assets such as NFTs, the cost varies but is usually in the 150-200 CKB range. For fully on-chain DOBs, the cost can easily exceed thousands of CKB.

The challenge is that when you send an asset to someone else, a cell must be created to hold it. This introduces additional costs to the sender if they pay the state rent for the receiver. However, there are multiple patterns to mitigate this depending on the situation.

Cell Model Asset Transfer Design Patterns

Several patterns can be used to address state rent costs for asset transfers. Each pattern balances simplicity, cost distribution, and trust requirements differently.

In the diagrams below, each box is a cell that holds assets and CKB capacity. A blue border marks a cell that is new or changed in that step. A yellow box is a cell with special rules, such as an ACP cell. Transaction fees are left out for simplicity.

Sender Pays State Rent Pattern

The sender covers all state rent costs for the receiver’s new cell. The asset transfer creates a cell owned by the receiver with capacity paid entirely by the sender.

Sender Pays State Rent Pattern. The task is to send 50 CAT coin to the receiver. Initial State: The sender has a regular cell with 200 CAT coin and 500 CKB. The receiver has no cells. After Transfer: The sender has a regular cell with 150 CAT coin and 358 CKB. The sender keeps the rest. The receiver has a regular cell with 50 CAT coin and 142 CKB. The sender paid for this cell.1040×754 48.6 KB

Pros:

  • Most simple and compatible method to implement.
  • No CKB requirements for receiver.
  • Single step process.

Cons:

  • Sender must pay extra CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Scales poorly as CKB price increases.
  • Costs create high barriers for frequent transfers.

Send and Refund Pattern

The sender pays state rent initially, then the receiver refunds the CKB capacity back to the sender. This requires trust on the part of the sender, and the receiver must actively participate after receiving the asset.

Send and Refund Pattern. The task is to send 50 DOG coin to the receiver. Initial State: The sender has a regular cell with 200 DOG coin and 500 CKB. The receiver has a regular cell with 300 CKB. After Transfer: The sender has a regular cell with 150 DOG coin and 358 CKB. The sender keeps the rest. The receiver has a regular cell with 50 DOG coin and 142 CKB. The sender paid for this cell. The receiver has a regular cell with 300 CKB. The sender now trusts the receiver to pay back 142 CKB. After Refund (Receiver Chooses to Pay Back): The sender has a regular cell with 150 DOG coin and 358 CKB. The sender has a regular cell with 142 CKB. The receiver refunded 142 CKB. The receiver has a regular cell with 50 DOG coin and 142 CKB. The receiver has a regular cell with 158 CKB. The receiver keeps the rest.1040×1366 88.6 KB

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Conceptually simple process that is easy to implement.

Cons:

  • Receiver must have CKB to pay the refund.
  • Receiver must be trusted to send back the CKB.
  • Requires automated bots for receiving applications.
  • No automated solutions exist for user to user transfers.

Anyone-Can-Pay (ACP) Pattern

The receiver creates a special cell which unlocks for any user when it detects that it is receiving additional assets, but remains securely locked in other scenarios. This is similar to a mail drop box, where anyone can make a deposit but it’s not possible to take anything back out.

The receiver must create an ACP cell ahead of time to hold the specific asset they want to receive. This only needs to be done once per asset, and then it can receive indefinitely.

Anyone-Can-Pay (ACP) Pattern. The task is to send 50 PIG coin to the receiver. Initial State: The sender has a regular cell with 200 PIG coin and 500 CKB. The receiver has a regular cell with 300 CKB. After ACP Cell Creation (One Time): The sender has a regular cell with 200 PIG coin and 500 CKB. The receiver has an ACP cell with 142 CKB. Anyone can add PIG coin. Only the receiver can take it. The receiver has a regular cell with 158 CKB. The receiver keeps the rest. After Transfer: The sender has a regular cell with 150 PIG coin and 500 CKB. The sender keeps all 500 CKB. The receiver has an ACP cell with 50 PIG coin and 142 CKB. The sender added the coins. The receiver did not sign. The receiver has a regular cell with 158 CKB.1040×1442 98.2 KB

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell (after refund).
  • Mature and tested pattern and implementation.
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must have CKB to create the ACP cell.
  • ACP cells must be pre-deployed by receivers for each asset.
  • Limited wallet and tooling support.
  • More complex smart contract logic.

Resources:

  • Anyone-Can-Pay Lock Script RFC - Official specification for ACP lock script.
  • Anyone-Can-Pay Repository - Current implementation and documentation.
  • OmniLock Repository - Advanced lock script that also supports anyone-can-pay functionality.

Cheque Cell Pattern

Implements a mechanism similar to a bank cheque where the sender creates a special cell that can be “cashed” by the receiver. The receiver must provide their own CKB capacity to claim the asset, and the CKB used for the cheque cell is returned to the sender. If the cheque remains unclaimed after 6 epochs, the sender can withdraw the assets and reclaim the capacity.

Cheque Cell Pattern. The task is to send 50 DUCK coin to the receiver. Initial State: The sender has a regular cell with 200 DUCK coin and 500 CKB. The receiver has a regular cell with 300 CKB. After Cheque Creation: The sender has a regular cell with 150 DUCK coin and 338 CKB. The sender keeps the rest. The receiver has a regular cell with 300 CKB. A new cheque cell holds 50 DUCK coin and 162 CKB. The receiver can claim it at any time. The sender can withdraw it only after 6 epochs (about 24 hours). Then one of two outcomes happens. Outcome A: Receiver Claims: The claim spends the cheque cell. The sender has a regular cell with 150 DUCK coin and 338 CKB. The sender has a regular cell with 162 CKB. The sender gets back 162 CKB. The receiver has a regular cell with 50 DUCK coin and 142 CKB. The receiver paid for this cell. The receiver has a regular cell with 158 CKB. The receiver keeps the rest. Outcome B: No Claim After 6 Epochs: The sender's withdrawal spends the cheque cell. The sender has a regular cell with 150 DUCK coin and 338 CKB. The sender has a regular cell with 50 DUCK coin and 162 CKB. The sender controls it again. The receiver has a regular cell with 300 CKB.1040×2114 229 KB

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Does not require the receiver to pre-deploy asset receiver cells.
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must have CKB to claim assets to a cell they own.
  • Unclaimed assets require the sender to undergo another step to recover.
  • Very limited wallet and tooling support.
  • More complex smart contract logic.

Resources:

  • Cheque Lock RFC - Official RFC specification for cheque lock, including example transactions.
  • Cheque Lock Script - Official cheque script implementation and documentation.

CoTA (Compact Token Aggregator) Pattern

CoTA is an NFT protocol which uses Sparse Merkle Trees (SMT) to manage large amounts of data off-chain while maintaining security guarantees on-chain. CoTA can be thought of as a layer 1.5 protocol that operates internally using the account-model, storing both data and ownership information in a distributed cell structure on top of UTXOs.

Each user creates a single permanent CoTA cell that becomes part of the distributed asset registry. Inside of each CoTA cell is a single SMT root hash consisting of exactly 32 bytes that provide provable information about the assets contained within the cell. The amount of data remains the same in a CoTA cell regardless of how many NFTs or how much data is associated with the user. An unlimited amount of NFTs can be created and held without increasing state rent costs.

CoTA builds on its distributed cell structure to add an innovative transfer mechanism that eliminate the immediate onboarding costs for new users to receive assets. CoTA assets operate on layer 1.5, which uses internal ownership tracking that is separate from the cell model. When assets are transferred on CoTA, they are marked for recipients without leaving the sender’s cell. This means that CoTA NFTs effectively bypass the state rent requirements, allowing NFTs to be minted for near-zero cost and can be sent to new users who hold no CKB. The caveat being that the receiver cannot transfer an NFT again until they complete the one-time CoTA cell registration process and complete the claim process which moves the NFT from the original sender’s CoTA cell to their own CoTA cell.

The CoTA transfer process involves four distinct stages:

Stage Sender Receiver Transfer Capability Notes
Initial Owns NFT No NFT Transferable The NFT is in the sender’s cell.
After Transfer No NFT Owns Unclaimed NFT Not Transferable Ownership is marked, and the NFT stays in the sender’s cell.
After Registration No NFT Owns Unclaimed NFT Not Transferable The receiver creates a CoTA cell to claim with. This step is optional.
After Claim No NFT Owns Claimed NFT Transferable The NFT is now in the receiver’s cell. This step is optional.

The registration process has a one-time fee of 150CKB, which is non-refundable since the cell that is created effectively becomes part of CoTA’s distributed cell structure. Registration is required to claim an NFT that has been marked for transfer, but it is not a requirement. Recipients will see unclaimed NFTs in their wallets just like normal NFTs, but they must register and claim if they want to send the NFT to someone else.

The following diagram illustrates how these stages work in practice with specific CKB capacity movements:

CoTA (Compact Token Aggregator) Pattern. The task is to send 1 FISH NFT to the receiver. Initial State: The sender has a CoTA cell with 150 CKB. It holds 1 FISH NFT. The receiver has a regular cell with 150 CKB. Aggregator: The sender owns 1 FISH NFT and can transfer it. After Transfer (Ownership Marked): The sender has a CoTA cell with 150 CKB. It records 1 FISH NFT as sent. The record stays as proof. The receiver has a regular cell with 150 CKB. No CKB is needed to receive. Aggregator: The receiver owns 1 FISH NFT but cannot transfer it yet. After Registration (Required to Claim; Optional): The sender has a CoTA cell with 150 CKB. It records 1 FISH NFT as sent. The receiver has a CoTA cell with 150 CKB. It was a regular cell before. Aggregator: The receiver owns 1 FISH NFT but cannot transfer it yet. After Claim (Optional): The sender has a CoTA cell with 150 CKB. It records 1 FISH NFT as sent. The claim used this record. The receiver has a CoTA cell with 150 CKB. It holds 1 FISH NFT. Aggregator: The receiver owns 1 FISH NFT and can transfer it.1040×1822 134 KB

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s CoTA cell.
  • Does not require the receiver to pre-deploy asset receiver cells.
  • Zero state rent cost for unclaimed transfers; claiming is not strictly required.
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must have CKB to register a CoTA cell before claiming.
  • CoTA’s layer 1.5 protocol has some incompatibilities with other protocols.
  • Requires an off-chain aggregator service for interpreting data.
  • Limited wallet and tooling support.
  • Transactions are more complex and must be generated using the CoTA SDK in conjunction with an aggregator.

Resources:

  • CoTA Protocol Overview - Official protocol documentation.
  • CoTA SDK JavaScript - JavaScript SDK for CoTA integration.
  • CoTA SDK Examples - Usage examples and integration guides.

Public Relay Cells Pattern (ACP Enhancement; Experimental)

Public relay cells are an optional enhancement to the Anyone-Can-Pay pattern that address the concurrency limitations by introducing public storage cells that act as temporary holding areas for token transfers. This pattern solves the collision problem where multiple simultaneous transfers to the same ACP cell would fail due to the deterministic nature of transfers on CKB.

In addition to increasing throughput to a single address by allowing parallel deposits, relay cells can serve as temporary holding areas for new users who haven’t yet deployed their own ACP cells. This allows new users to receive tokens without any upfront CKB requirement, dramatically lowering the barrier to entry into the ecosystem.

The relay cells are serviced by a decentralized network of fulfillment bots that monitor deposits and deliver tokens to their final destinations. These bots compete to process transfers, earning small fees for providing this collection and delivery service. This creates a permissionless marketplace where anyone can operate a fulfillment bot, ensuring system resilience without single points of failure while creating earning opportunities for operators providing fulfillment services.

Public Relay Cells Pattern. The task is to send 50 BIRD coin to the receiver. Initial State: The sender has a regular cell with 200 BIRD coin and 500 CKB. The receiver has an ACP cell with 142 CKB. It is empty. Anyone can deposit to any relay cell, and service bots deliver. Relay cell 1 has 142 CKB. Relay cell 2 has 142 CKB. Relay cell 3 has 142 CKB. After Deposit to Relay: The sender has a regular cell with 150 BIRD coin and 500 CKB. The sender keeps the rest. The receiver has an ACP cell with 142 CKB. Relay cell 1 has 50 BIRD coin and 142 CKB. It is marked for the receiver. Relay cell 2 has 142 CKB. Relay cell 3 has 142 CKB. After a Service Bot Delivers: The sender has a regular cell with 150 BIRD coin and 500 CKB. The receiver has an ACP cell with 50 BIRD coin and 142 CKB. A bot delivered the coins. Relay cell 1 has 142 CKB. It is empty again. Relay cell 2 has 142 CKB. Relay cell 3 has 142 CKB.1040×1824 138 KB

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Does not require the receiver to pre-deploy asset receiver cells (ACP cells).
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must eventually have CKB to claim assets to a cell they own.
  • Unclaimed assets may be returned or forfeited.
  • Emerging incomplete standard with no implementation.

Challenges:
As this standard is still a work in progress, several challenges remain to be addressed. One concern is the potential for relay cell clogging if tokens remain unclaimed for extended periods. Proposed solutions include implementing asset forfeiture mechanisms after certain timeframes, which would incentivize timely claiming while preventing permanent blockage of relay resources.

Resources:

  • Public Relay Cells Discussion - Original proposal and community discussion on Nervos Talk.

Harbor Pattern (Fractal Standard; Experimental)

Harbor is a pattern within the Fractal token standard which is currently in early development stages. The Fractal standard takes inspiration from CoTA, using Sparse Merkle Trees (SMT) to manage asset data off-chain while maintaining security guarantees on-chain. However, Fractal utilizes the Cell Model for ownership designation instead of a layer 1.5 account model structure. Harbors have similarities to public relay cells in being publicly available areas for asset storage, but Harbors can be used both as temporary storage and permanent storage.

A Fractal cell contains a single SMT root hash consisting of exactly 32 bytes, similar to a CoTA cell. The amount of data always remains the same regardless of how many assets are associated with the user, allowing for an unlimited amount of assets to be held without increasing state rent costs. A Fractal cell uses normal locks and allows the owner to control all assets within the cell.

A Harbor cell is a special kind of Fractal cell, which is created by anyone for public use. Anyone can store a Fractal asset in any Harbor by paying a small “parking fee” to the operator. Multiple Harbors can be created by anyone to create a competitive marketplace that keeps fees reasonable while providing parallelism for concurrent transfers. Should an operator wish to close their Harbor to recoup the CKB being used for state rent, they are free to do so at any time. However, if there are any Fractal assets stored within the harbor they are trying to close, they must migrate them to another open harbor and pay the parking fee for each asset.

Harbor cells can serve as holding areas for new users who haven’t yet acquired any CKB to create their own Fractal cell, allowing them to bypass the state rent requirements. Since Fractal cells can hold any number of assets, they never will experience a “clogging” scenario that could happen with a public relay cell. For this reason, a Fractal cell is suitable for permanent storage. However, some smart contracts may not be able to operate normally with assets in a Harbor, and may still require withdrawal to a normal Fractal cell.

Note: The Fractal standard and Harbor pattern are in very early development and specifications may change significantly.

The Harbor transfer process involves up to four distinct stages:

Stage Sender Receiver Transfer Capability Notes
Initial Owns Assets No Assets Transferable The assets are in the sender’s cell or a Harbor cell.
After Transfer No Assets Owns Assets in Harbor Transferable Ownership is marked, and the assets move to a Harbor cell.
After Registration No Assets Owns Assets in Harbor Transferable The receiver creates a Fractal cell to claim with. This step is optional.
After Claim No Assets Owns Assets Transferable The assets move to the receiver’s cell. This step is optional.

The registration process requires 150CKB to create a Fractal cell, which is refundable if the cell is later destroyed. Registration is required to claim assets that have been stored in a Harbor, but it is not strictly necessary for ownership. Recipients use Harbor-stored assets as if they were holding them directly and can transfer them to other users as needed.

The following diagram illustrates how these stages work in practice with specific CKB capacity movements:

Harbor Pattern (Fractal Standard). The task is to send 75 WOLF coin to the receiver. Initial State: The sender has a Fractal cell with 150 CKB. It holds 75 WOLF coin. The receiver has a regular cell with 150 CKB. A Harbor cell has 150 CKB. The Harbor operator owns this cell. It holds no assets yet. Anyone can park assets here for a small fee. Aggregator: The sender owns 75 WOLF coin and can transfer it. After Transfer to Harbor: The sender has a Fractal cell with 150 CKB. It holds 0 WOLF coin. The assets moved to the Harbor. The receiver has a regular cell with 150 CKB. No CKB is needed to receive. A Harbor cell has 150 CKB. The Harbor operator owns this cell. It holds 75 WOLF coin for the receiver. Aggregator: The receiver can transfer 75 WOLF coin in the Harbor. After Registration (Required to Claim; Optional): The sender has a Fractal cell with 150 CKB. It holds 0 WOLF coin. The receiver has a Fractal cell with 150 CKB. It holds 0 WOLF coin. It was a regular cell before. A Harbor cell has 150 CKB. The Harbor operator owns this cell. It holds 75 WOLF coin for the receiver. Aggregator: The receiver can transfer 75 WOLF coin in the Harbor. After Claim (Optional): The sender has a Fractal cell with 150 CKB. It holds 0 WOLF coin. The receiver has a Fractal cell with 150 CKB. It holds 75 WOLF coin. The coins came from the Harbor. A Harbor cell has 150 CKB. The Harbor operator owns this cell. It holds no assets. Aggregator: The receiver owns 75 WOLF coin and can transfer it.1040×2886 306 KB

Pros:

  • Sender does not pay the CKB for the receiver’s cell.
  • Does not require the receiver to pre-deploy asset receiver cells.
  • No trust requirements.

Cons:

  • Receiver must eventually have CKB to claim assets to a cell they own.
  • Requires an off-chain aggregator service for interpreting data.
  • Transactions are more complex and must be generated using the Fractal SDK in conjunction with an aggregator.
  • Emerging incomplete standard with no implementation.

Closing

The Cell Model’s state rent requirement creates unique challenges for asset transfers that have sparked innovative design patterns that offer different trade-offs between simplicity, cost, trust, and user experience.

This document explores seven distinct transfer patterns for addressing state rent challenges in UTXO-based asset transfers:

  1. Sender Pays State Rent - The most straightforward approach where senders cover all capacity costs for receivers’ new cells. While simple to implement and requiring no CKB from receivers, it scales poorly as CKB prices increase and creates barriers for frequent transfers.

  2. Send and Refund - A trust-based pattern where senders initially pay state rent, then receivers refund the capacity. Conceptually simple but requires active receiver participation and trust, with limited automated solutions for user-to-user transfers.

  3. Anyone-Can-Pay (ACP) - A mature, trustless solution using special cells that unlock when receiving assets. Requires receivers to pre-deploy cells for each asset type and has concurrency limitations, but offers proven reliability for users.

  4. Cheque Cell - Implements a bank cheque-like mechanism where senders create claimable cells with automatic withdrawal after timeout. Provides trustless transfers without pre-deployment requirements but adds complexity for managing unclaimed assets.

  5. CoTA (Compact Token Aggregator) - An innovative layer 1.5 protocol using Sparse Merkle Trees for off-chain data management. Virtually eliminates state rent for unclaimed transfers and allows near zero-cost minting, but requires off-chain aggregator infrastructure and has protocol incompatibilities.

  6. Public Relay Cells (Experimental) - An ACP enhancement using intermediate public storage cells to address concurrency limitations. Enables parallel deposits and serves new users without upfront CKB requirements, but relies on decentralized fulfillment bots and remains in experimental stages.

  7. Harbor (Fractal Standard; Experimental) - An emerging pattern within the Fractal token standard that combines the use of Sparse Merkle Trees for off-chain data management with decentralized public cells for asset storage. Allows for near zero-cost minting and eliminates state rent for newly onboarded users. However, the standard is in very early development with no current implementation.

Which Pattern to Use?

For Simple Applications:

  • Use “Sender Pays State Rent” for low-volume transfers where simplicity matters most.
  • Consider “Send and Refund” for applications which inherently require trust and the pattern offers few drawbacks.

For Production Applications:

  • Choose “Anyone-Can-Pay” for mature applications where deposits are made to an application where pre-deploying ACP cells is possible.
  • Select “Cheque Cell” when receivers cannot pre-deploy cells but trustless transfers are essential.
  • Consider “CoTA” for NFT applications where low-cost NFTs and unclaimed transfers provide significant user experience benefits.

For Future Applications:

  • Evaluate “Public Relay Cells” as a solution to scale ACP’s concurrency limitations.
  • Monitor “Harbor” development for future ultra-low-cost asset solutions.

recent_posts.author: JackyLHH
recent_posts.content_text:
Question Time Xiaomao noir1920×1080 710 KB
Noir CKB is a developer toolchain that connects the Noir programming language (for writing zero-knowledge proofs) with the Nervos CKB blockchain.
In simple terms:
Imagine you want to keep a secret number (like a private score or balance) stored on a blockchain, where only you should be able to update it, without ever revealing the number itself.
Noir CKB is an experimental way to write private logic in the relatively friendly Noir language, and safely enforce it on CKB. The Private Tally is the current live demo, you can try on testnet if you want to experiment.
Noir is a programming language made for zero-knowledge (ZK) proofs. ZK proofs let you prove “I followed the rules correctly” (e.g., “I added 5 to my secret number”) without showing the secret. Noir has a clean, Rust-like syntax, so it’s more approachable than older ZK languages. Noir was created by Aztec Network.
CKB (Common Knowledge Base) is the Layer 1 blockchain of the Nervos Network. It is Bitcoin-inspired (Proof-of-Work, UTXO-style) but flexible and highly programmable. Data lives in “cells,” and small programs called scripts decide how those cells can be updated. Scripts run in CKB-VM (a RISC-V virtual machine).
Noir CKB lets you:
Write the rule in Noir (e.g. “new secret = old secret + amount I add”).
Generate a ZK proof on your own computer.
Submit a transaction on CKB. A Type Script on-chain verifies the proof and checks that the proof is specifically about this cell and this exact state change (right network, right old commitment, right new commitment, etc.).
The key idea of the project is:
“A proof that verifies is not the same as a proof that authorizes this cell transition.”
Xiaomao.
A mathematically perfect proof could still be about the wrong cell or update. Noir CKB binds the proof tightly to the actual transaction so it can’t be reused incorrectly.
The Private Tally is a cell that holds a hidden number.
Only the person with the secret key can add to it.
Every update is authorized by a zero-knowledge proof generated on their machine.
The cell stores only a commitment (a fingerprint of the number + fresh randomness), so the real value stays private.
You can add any amount, including 0.
There is no normal signature lock; the proof itself is the authority.
On-chain the updates look the same whether you added something or nothing. What stays private is the actual value and the amounts added. Transaction metadata (existence of the tally, timing, who paid fees) is still visible.
It is research / experimental software (pre-audit, testnet only). Not for production or mainnet use yet.
Below is a set of questions targeting the core design trade-offs (binding correctness, performance, trust, tooling, and privacy limits) rather than surface-level features.
We want to pick Xiaomao’s brain on Noir CKB so here it goes:
Hello hello Xiaomao, how’s things? Let’s start with a personal statement, shall we? Who are you, and what is your background?
“My name is Xiaomao, and I’m a ZK and privacy engineer.”
“Most of my work sits in the zero-knowledge and privacy space, what pulls me in is the idea that you can prove something is true without revealing the data behind it. I think privacy is one of the most important problems in this industry. As more of our lives move on-chain, everything being public by default stops being acceptable, and I want to build the tooling that lets people keep private what should stay private, while still proving they followed the rules.”
“For about a year, I worked with Base as a developer in East Africa, where I helped developers get started, ran workshops, and supported the local builder community. These days my focus has gone deeper into the ZK and cryptography side, and I’m building on CKB. If I had to put my focus in one line, it’s privacy, and the practical side of it: bridging the gap between what protocols can do and what builders can actually ship. A lot of powerful cryptography never reaches developers because the distance between the research and a working build is too wide, and closing that gap is the work I care about most.”
“Outside of engineering, community is a big part of what I do. I co-founded LedgerLady, a women-led developer community that trains and equips women to become strong Web3 developers, and we run cohorts and university workshops across East Africa. I’m also an open-source enthusiast and contributor, so a lot of what I build and learn happens in the open.”
Wonderful, I can see you’ve been busy. How did you find out about CKBuilders and what is it like working around other CKBuilders? What interests you about CKB?
“I found CKB through a friend, to be honest. We were just chatting and he told me about a protocol called CKB, which had a builders program, and they asked if I wanted to join. I said sure, and he referred me to Neon, who leads CKBuilders. After talking with Neon I was onboarded, and that’s really when I started learning what CKB is. I hadn’t come across it on my own before that.”
“It’s been a really good experience. Beyond learning CKB itself, the part I didn’t expect to enjoy so much is watching other builders grow and seeing the range of things people are shipping in the CKB space. One thing I found fascinating is that most of us coming in as new CKB devs, came from somewhere else first. Some came from Ethereum, some from Polkadot, some from Bitcoin. Noir CKB is a developer toolchain that connects the Noir programming language (for writing zero-knowledge proofs) with the Nervos CKB blockchain.

In simple terms:

Imagine you want to keep a secret number (like a private score or balance) stored on a blockchain, where only you should be able to update it, without ever revealing the number itself.

Noir CKB is an experimental way to write private logic in the relatively friendly Noir language, and safely enforce it on CKB. The Private Tally is the current live demo, you can try on testnet if you want to experiment.

  • Noir is a programming language made for zero-knowledge (ZK) proofs. ZK proofs let you prove “I followed the rules correctly” (e.g., “I added 5 to my secret number”) without showing the secret. Noir has a clean, Rust-like syntax, so it’s more approachable than older ZK languages. Noir was created by Aztec Network.
  • CKB (Common Knowledge Base) is the Layer 1 blockchain of the Nervos Network. It is Bitcoin-inspired (Proof-of-Work, UTXO-style) but flexible and highly programmable. Data lives in “cells,” and small programs called scripts decide how those cells can be updated. Scripts run in CKB-VM (a RISC-V virtual machine).

Noir CKB lets you:

  • Write the rule in Noir (e.g. “new secret = old secret + amount I add”).
  • Generate a ZK proof on your own computer.
  • Submit a transaction on CKB. A Type Script on-chain verifies the proof and checks that the proof is specifically about this cell and this exact state change (right network, right old commitment, right new commitment, etc.).

“A proof that verifies is not the same as a proof that authorizes this cell transition.”

Xiaomao.

A mathematically perfect proof could still be about the wrong cell or update. Noir CKB binds the proof tightly to the actual transaction so it can’t be reused incorrectly.

The way I think about it is that Noir CKB is for making specific pieces of state private and provably correct, not for making an entire system invisible.”

Great answers, Xiaomao! Thank you for taking the time to answer these questions. What are your next steps or plans for continued development on CKB?

“In the short term, I’m finishing the research that de-risks the hard parts, so the next things I build stand on tested ground rather than hope. The first real application I want to ship on top of that is a private ballot box, where each vote is a hidden update that the chain can count and verify without ever seeing who voted for what. Alongside that, I’m hardening the proof-to-transition binding with the generator and its test matrix.”

“I’m also contributing improvements back upstream to the Groth16 verifier that Cecilia Mulandi built, which is the on-chain verifier my whole project depends on. The main improvement is a single-product rewrite of the pairing check that cuts a flat 20 million cycles or so off every verification, along with the tighter checks that came out of reviewing it. The reason that matters is that it isn’t only my project that gets cheaper. Anyone doing Groth16 verification on CKB uses less of the block’s cycle budget, so the whole ZK stack on CKB gets a little more practical, not just Noir CKB.”

“The bigger vision is this. Right now, building a private, proof-authorized application on CKB means being both a ZK engineer and a CKB script engineer, and hand-writing the binding logic that ties a proof to an exact state transition, which is the part that’s easiest to get subtly wrong. I want to collapse that. The goal is a toolkit where a developer brings their own Noir circuit and a small, readable spec, and gets back a correct, auditable CKB type script, the artifacts, and the adversarial tests, generated for them. If that works, privacy on CKB stops being something only a handful of specialists can build, and becomes something any capable developer can reach for. That’s the thread running through everything I do, closing the gap between what the cryptography can do and what builders can actually ship. The Nervos community DAO grant work I gained after, is me building that bridge for privacy on CKB. Longer term, I want this to grow into a broader base of open privacy and ZK infrastructure and research on CKB that other people build on, not a single app that stops with me.”

Thank you, Xiaomao, for all your answers and your work among the CKB community and through the CKBuilders initiative. These interviews and projects are vital for ecosystem growth, and to help others understand CKB and the possibilities around ZK proofs.

recent_posts.content_text:
What happens to a reusable package as it moves through borrowing, return, and reuse—and what can CKB actually verify about that journey? ReuseLoop is a CKB Testnet prototype that records an item’s administrator-authorized state changes: AVAILABLE → BORROWED → RETURNED → AVAILABLE.
CKB records application state and authorized transitions. Physical handoffs, returns, cleaning, and inspections happen off-chain and are not proven by the chain.
Workflow overview
The diagram separates the current read-only walkthrough from the lifecycle modeled by the prototype.
flowchart TD
subgraph Demo["Current walkthrough: read-only"]

Read --> View["Operator sees current status and available action"]
end
subgraph Lifecycle["Lifecycle represented"]
Available["AVAILABLE"] -->|Borrow| Borrowed["BORROWED"]
Borrowed -->|Confirm return| Returned["RETURNED"]
Returned -->|Make available| Available

Physical["Handoff, return, cleaning, inspection"] -.-> Offchain["Off-chain events are not proven by CKB state"]
How the transaction path works
An operator selects an allowed state transition and reviews its preview. One configured administrator approves it in JoyID. The app submits the signed transaction to CKB Testnet, tracks confirmation, then refreshes the item state and history.
The current walkthrough is read-only: it reuses an existing Registry and item and submits no new lifecycle transaction. CKB Lock Scripts verify the administrator’s signature; Type Scripts enforce Registry membership and valid transitions. The MVP has no separate borrower or store keys and no multi-party authorization.

topics.title: CellScript Roadmap: Expanding the Frontier of CKB-Native DeFi

recent_posts.topic_title: CellScript Roadmap: Expanding the Frontier of CKB-Native DeFi
recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
Part 2 Completion
Part 2 of the roadmap, Basic Pools, Orders and Settlement, has completed bounded validation on the CellScript 0.36 development line.
The examples now cover constant-product pools, LP deposits and redemptions, escrowed orders with partial fills and cancellation, atomic order-to-pool settlement, shared payments, and two-pool routing.
The acceptance runs replayed 282 archived transactions and committed 60 transactions on a pinned local CKB node. Finance packages · Acceptance record
What does writing a swap look like?
Start by describing which Cells the transaction spends and what must replace them. A swap spends the current pool state, the two reserve Cells tied to it, and the trader’s funding Cells. It creates the next pool state and reserves, gives the trader the purchased asset, and returns any change. That input-to-output transition is what the scripts verify. CKB Cell Model
Suppose the pool holds 1,000 A and 2,000 B. A trader swaps 100 A with a minimum receive of 180 B. At a fee of 30 basis points, the integer quote is 181 B. These are the lines that compute it in the example pool Lock. a and b are the old reserves, and a_max is the exact A input in this swap mode.
let scaled = a_max * (10000 - fee) as u128;
let received = mul_div_floor(b, scaled, a * 10000 + scaled);
The Lock checks that the actual successor reserves are 1,100 A and 1,819 B, that the trader’s B output includes the quoted 181 B, and that LP supply stays the same. The asset and reserve scripts verify their own rules against the same transaction. This is how the quote becomes an enforceable trade. Pool verifier
How to start building
Write the state transition in CellScript. Define the Cell data and validation rules in an ordinary .cell package. For a pool or order, spell out the accepted asset identities, rounding, who receives payment, and which balances must be preserved or updated. Protocol examples
Build the transaction off-chain. Resolve the live input Cells and the deployed script dependencies, encode Cell data and witnesses with the generated encoders, then sign, dry-run, and submit. The SDK example runs this path against a disposable CKB node. Builder example
Test the whole transaction. From a 0.36 checkout with the SDK guide’s prerequisites, the finance protocol suite gives you working pool and settlement cases to modify. Try raising the minimum receive above the quote and observe which script rejects the transaction.
cargo test --locked -p cellscript --test finance_protocol
The keeper discussion fits here. An order can sit in escrow until a wallet, bot, or independent keeper adapter submits a fill. The submitter handles when and how to send the transaction. The scripts check who gets paid, how much escrow remains, and whether the proposed fill follows the order’s terms. Order package

recent_posts.topic_title: CKB x Kaze Unitour Phase 2 Kicks Off at Machakos University: 180+ Students, 95 New Wallets
recent_posts.author: Dorex45
recent_posts.content_text:
Phase 2 of the CKB x Kaze Unitour began on Thursday, 19 November at Machakos University, and the turnout exceeded what we planned for. More than 180 students joined us for three hours of hands-on learning, and 95 of them left with a brand new self-custodial wallet on Kaze.
17954612245561392×928 170 KB
Why we run the Unitour
Most students in Kenya have heard of Bitcoin, but very few have actually held their own keys. The Unitour exists to close that gap. We take Bitcoin and CKB education directly to campuses, and we make sure everyone leaves having done something real rather than just listened.
What we covered
The session ran from 14:00 to 17:00 and followed the same flow we use on every stop:
Bitcoin 101: what Bitcoin is, why it matters in Africa, and what self-custody really means
CKB and Nervos: the Layer 1 behind Kaze, including RGB++ and the Fiber Network
Kaze: how contributors earn CKB for every approved location they map, and how they can cash out to M-Pesa
Live wallet setup: students installed Kaze and created their own wallets in the room, step by step with our team
Live mapping: students added real places around campus and followed the leaderboard as pins were approved
17954612245111600×1066 288 KB
17954612245281920×1280 407 KB
The numbers
180+ attendees
95 new wallets created
First stop of Phase 2, following the earlier stops of the tour
17954612245471392×928 131 KB
What stood out
The live setup was the best part of the afternoon. Seeing a room of students create wallets at the same time, ask questions about their recovery phrases, and then start mapping places they walk past every day made the idea feel tangible. The question we heard most was how to cash out to M-Pesa, which shows how much the local offramp matters for adoption.
Challenges
No event runs perfectly, and we want to be open about what we had to solve on the day.
A turnout bigger than planned. We prepared for a smaller room, and more than 180 students came. A crowd that size is a good problem to have, but it stretched our space, our team and the one-on-one help we could give during wallet setup.
Our main videographer fell sick on the day. Our lead videographer could not make it, and with little notice we paired up with a student videographer from the university. Working from our shooting SOP guides, the student captured the raw footage, and we are sending it to our main videographer to edit into the final content. This is why highlights from the event will land a little later than usual.
Thank you
Thank you to Machakos University and the students who showed up with curiosity and energy, and to the Nervos community for the continued support behind the tour: @NervosNetwork, @ckbsamurai, @NervosNation and @ckba_build.
What’s next
The Unitour continues across Kenyan campuses. If you are a student, a club lead or a community builder and want the tour at your university, reach out to us at business@usekaze.app or on X at @usekaze. If you attended and want to keep learning, join the Kaze and CKB community groups and tell us what you want to see next.
You can download Kaze at usekaze.app.

recent_posts.content_text:
gm @neon.bit @zz_tovarishch and everyone. I urge the Community Fund DAO to pause its decision on this proposal until the applicant’s identity, affiliations, grant history and event claims have been independently verified.
The concern is the combination of records: an Arbitrum grant case in which Questbook identified the NexusPay/UmojaVerse team in connection with impersonation; public records identifying Griffins Oduol alias (FidelCoder) as a NexusPay/UmojaVerse co-founder; an ETHSafari grant application that names Oduol alias (FidelCoder) and links his personal accounts; and a CKB application making substantial reach claims without providing underlying attendance records. Taken together, these warrant serious scrutiny before community funds are committed.
1. Questbook documented impersonation in an Arbitrum grant case
In its public review of Arbitrum’s Questbook grants [https:// forum.arbitrum.foundation/t/questbook-dda-program-report/27859], Entropy reported that the people behind a $25,000 Stylus AI Auditor grant impersonated Zak Micallef and Carlos Felici. Entropy said both confirmed that they were not involved.
Questbook’s program manager later described the incident and the investigation [ https:// forum.arbitrum.foundation/t/questbook-dda-program-report/27859/1 ]. The manager said the NexusPay/UmojaVerse team was behind the impersonation and had submitted proposals in other Questbook grant areas. Questbook reported that the $25,000 grant had been paid. The program manager also said the delivered product was essentially a ChatGPT wrapper and its reported growth metrics were inaccurate.
This is a documented finding by the grant programme’s reviewers and manager, not simply a social media accusation.
2. Public records directly connect Griffins Oduol to NexusPay and Umojaverse
Griffins Oduol publicly described himself as a NexusPay/Umojaverse co-founder. The Arbitrum Get Going @ETHSafari application [ https:// questbook.app/dashboard/?proposalId=6879604e3c1bac3fce7627f2&grantId=67d8021646da2f90cc325521&role=community&chainId=10&isRenderingProposalBody=true ] names Griffins Oduol as a team member
Those are direct identity links in the application, not a resemblance between unrelated accounts. They tie the ETHSafari application to Oduol and Umojaverse, and the public NexusPay sources tie Oduol to the team Questbook identified.
This establishes a direct organizational connection. It does not by itself prove which individual submitted or carried out every act in the impersonation case. The CKB DAO should require Oduol to disclose his role in NexusPay and answer whether he or any Umojaverse team member participated in the grant applications Questbook described.
3. The ETHSafari application’s claims and authorization need checking
The application requested $25,000 for an “Arbitrum Get Going @ETHSafariETHSafariETHSafariETHSafari 2025” programme. It used ETHSafari event information and its deck, and represented that an Arbitrum Ambassador had confirmed participation. The applicant listed Oduol’s personal accounts and Umojaverse as part of the team.
SEEDGov ultimately rejected the proposal, citing concerns about the feasibility of its KPIs and the budget. The rejection itself is not a finding of fraud. However, the application’s use of ETHSafari’s name, materials and claimed participation should be checked directly with ETHSafari and each named participant.
4. A separate Arbitrum application placed Griffins Oduol, NexusPay and Shem Okeyo on the same team
In a separate Arbitrum proposal for the Burstek DAO Initiative [https:// forum.arbitrum.foundation/t/burstek-dao-initiative-advancing-africas-blockchain-frontier-with-arbitrum/20505 ], the application identifies Griffins Oduol and Nashons Agate as NexusPay co-founders and lists Shem Okeyo among the team. This establishes that they were named together in a prior grant application; it does not, on its own, establish wrongdoing by Oduol.
Because other records in the supplied materials concern Arbitrum proposals involving Shem Okeyo, the CKB DAO should ask the applicant to disclose the extent and dates of any working relationship and provide the relevant grant reports. The committee should assess each record on its own evidence.
5. The CKB proposal’s reach claims need primary evidence
The CKB application claims a campus programme reached 503 developers, generated 104 project ideas and produced 23 hackerhouse submissions. It also claims a five-country Pulse East Africa HackFest with at least 90 participants per country. The proposal’s own “Previous work” section does not provide underlying attendance records for these totals.
Oduol’s Arbitrum Builders Initiative final report reports that Umojaverse received $16,840 and describes the earlier campus programme. The CKB proposal should link to the award and final report, explain how the reported figures were calculated, and provide dated event evidence and partner confirmations for the five-country claim. Until that documentation is supplied, the CKB reach numbers are unverified.
6. ChainWeb’s Zcash application raises a separate identity-consent concern
In Zcash Community Grants application #474 [ https://-github-com/ZcashCommunityGrants/zcashcommunitygrants/issues/474 ] , ChainWeb named Rust and WebAssembly developer Njuguna Mureithi as technical support. Mureithi replied publicly that he did not know the applicants and had not been involved, and called the use of his name fraud.
This is a serious allegation about the ChainWeb application. I have not seen conclusive evidence that ChainWeb is part of Oduol’s team, so I am not presenting it as such. The CKB committee should verify all named affiliations directly and should not treat separate applications as proof of a shared team without evidence.
7. Why this matters for Nairobi and African Web3
When grant money is awarded on the strength of claimed team credentials, partnerships and participant numbers, impersonation and unsupported reporting do more than waste one grant. They divert limited ecosystem funding from builders who can deliver, weaken trust between local communities and international protocols, and make future reviewers more cautious about funding African projects.
That can raise the burden on legitimate Nairobi and African teams: more verification, slower decisions and greater difficulty establishing credibility with sponsors, mentors and users. It also risks damaging the communities whose names and event networks are used to make proposals look credible. For this reason, verifying identities, consent, grant history and reach claims protects both the CKB treasury and the reputation of African Web3 builders.
Requested checks before any funding decision
Verify Oduol’s identity and obtain direct confirmation from every instructor, mentor, judge and partner named in the CKB proposal.
Require a complete disclosure of Umojaverse’s and Oduol’s grant applications, awards, payments and final reports, including the Arbitrum grants.
Ask Oduol to explain his NexusPay role in light of Questbook’s documented investigation and whether he or Umojaverse personnel were involved in the proposals it discussed.
Ask ETHSafari and the Arbitrum participants named in the ETHSafari proposal to confirm whether they authorized or agreed to the proposed participation.
Require dated, independently checkable evidence for the CKB proposal’s campus and five-country participant counts.
If the DAO funds the programme, tie payments to independently verifiable milestones and pay prizes directly to winners after eligibility is confirmed.
The records establish a serious NexusPay/UmojaVerse connection to a documented grant impersonation case, direct links between Griffins Oduol alias (FidelCoder) and the ETHSafari application, and prior grant activity that should be fully disclosed. They also raise questions about unverified CKB reach claims. The DAO should resolve these points before committing funds.

This is a documented finding by the grant programme’s reviewers and manager, not simply a social media accusation.

2. Public records directly connect Griffins Oduol to NexusPay and Umojaverse

Griffins Oduol publicly described himself as a NexusPay/Umojaverse co-founder. The Arbitrum Get Going @ETHSafari application [ https:// questbook.app/dashboard/?proposalId=6879604e3c1bac3fce7627f2&grantId=67d8021646da2f90cc325521&role=community&chainId=10&isRenderingProposalBody=true ] names Griffins Oduol as a team member

Those are direct identity links in the application, not a resemblance between unrelated accounts. They tie the ETHSafari application to Oduol and Umojaverse, and the public NexusPay sources tie Oduol to the team Questbook identified.

This establishes a direct organizational connection. It does not by itself prove which individual submitted or carried out every act in the impersonation case. The CKB DAO should require Oduol to disclose his role in NexusPay and answer whether he or any Umojaverse team member participated in the grant applications Questbook described.

3. The ETHSafari application’s claims and authorization need checking

The application requested $25,000 for an “Arbitrum Get Going @ETHSafariETHSafariETHSafariETHSafari 2025” programme. It used ETHSafari event information and its deck, and represented that an Arbitrum Ambassador had confirmed participation. The applicant listed Oduol’s personal accounts and Umojaverse as part of the team.

SEEDGov ultimately rejected the proposal, citing concerns about the feasibility of its KPIs and the budget. The rejection itself is not a finding of fraud. However, the application’s use of ETHSafari’s name, materials and claimed participation should be checked directly with ETHSafari and each named participant.

4. A separate Arbitrum application placed Griffins Oduol, NexusPay and Shem Okeyo on the same team

In a separate Arbitrum proposal for the Burstek DAO Initiative [https:// forum.arbitrum.foundation/t/burstek-dao-initiative-advancing-africas-blockchain-frontier-with-arbitrum/20505 ], the application identifies Griffins Oduol and Nashons Agate as NexusPay co-founders and lists Shem Okeyo among the team. This establishes that they were named together in a prior grant application; it does not, on its own, establish wrongdoing by Oduol.

Because other records in the supplied materials concern Arbitrum proposals involving Shem Okeyo, the CKB DAO should ask the applicant to disclose the extent and dates of any working relationship and provide the relevant grant reports. The committee should assess each record on its own evidence.

5. The CKB proposal’s reach claims need primary evidence

The CKB application claims a campus programme reached 503 developers, generated 104 project ideas and produced 23 hackerhouse submissions. It also claims a five-country Pulse East Africa HackFest with at least 90 participants per country. The proposal’s own “Previous work” section does not provide underlying attendance records for these totals.

Oduol’s Arbitrum Builders Initiative final report reports that Umojaverse received $16,840 and describes the earlier campus programme. The CKB proposal should link to the award and final report, explain how the reported figures were calculated, and provide dated event evidence and partner confirmations for the five-country claim. Until that documentation is supplied, the CKB reach numbers are unverified.

6. ChainWeb’s Zcash application raises a separate identity-consent concern

In Zcash Community Grants application #474 [ https://-github-com/ZcashCommunityGrants/zcashcommunitygrants/issues/474 ] , ChainWeb named Rust and WebAssembly developer Njuguna Mureithi as technical support. Mureithi replied publicly that he did not know the applicants and had not been involved, and called the use of his name fraud.

This is a serious allegation about the ChainWeb application. I have not seen conclusive evidence that ChainWeb is part of Oduol’s team, so I am not presenting it as such. The CKB committee should verify all named affiliations directly and should not treat separate applications as proof of a shared team without evidence.

7. Why this matters for Nairobi and African Web3

When grant money is awarded on the strength of claimed team credentials, partnerships and participant numbers, impersonation and unsupported reporting do more than waste one grant. They divert limited ecosystem funding from builders who can deliver, weaken trust between local communities and international protocols, and make future reviewers more cautious about funding African projects.

That can raise the burden on legitimate Nairobi and African teams: more verification, slower decisions and greater difficulty establishing credibility with sponsors, mentors and users. It also risks damaging the communities whose names and event networks are used to make proposals look credible. For this reason, verifying identities, consent, grant history and reach claims protects both the CKB treasury and the reputation of African Web3 builders.

Requested checks before any funding decision

  1. Verify Oduol’s identity and obtain direct confirmation from every instructor, mentor, judge and partner named in the CKB proposal.

  2. Require a complete disclosure of Umojaverse’s and Oduol’s grant applications, awards, payments and final reports, including the Arbitrum grants.

  3. Ask Oduol to explain his NexusPay role in light of Questbook’s documented investigation and whether he or Umojaverse personnel were involved in the proposals it discussed.

  4. Ask ETHSafari and the Arbitrum participants named in the ETHSafari proposal to confirm whether they authorized or agreed to the proposed participation.

  5. Require dated, independently checkable evidence for the CKB proposal’s campus and five-country participant counts.

  6. If the DAO funds the programme, tie payments to independently verifiable milestones and pay prizes directly to winners after eligibility is confirmed.

The records establish a serious NexusPay/UmojaVerse connection to a documented grant impersonation case, direct links between Griffins Oduol alias (FidelCoder) and the ETHSafari application, and prior grant activity that should be fully disclosed. They also raise questions about unverified CKB reach claims. The DAO should resolve these points before committing funds.

recent_posts.content_text:
ckb-whitehat — Spark Program application
Status: ready to run (tool shipped at v0.4.2). The repository
(https://github.com/nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat)
already exists under my GitHub account (nghiadang391) and holds two completed
pilots plus a working Go CLI release (v0.4.2, CI green). This application
funds the first systematic whitehat verification of three more CKB-DAO-funded
CKB/Fiber money products, plus three net-new forward deliverables on the tool
itself. Code for each new target lands in this repo week by week, with its
FINDINGS.md, its deterministic PoC suite, and its patch packs.
License: MIT.
Title: Spark Program | ckb-whitehat: deterministic whitehat verification of CKB/Fiber money products — AI-assisted triage, replayable PoCs, patches, consent-based disclosure
Category: DAOs & Funding → Spark Program (posted directly in the Spark sub-section per the 2026-07-19 forum update)
1. Project overview
Project name: ckb-whitehat
Repository: https://github.com/nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat (latest release: v0.4.2, MIT)
One-sentence summary: ckb-whitehat is a shipped community verification
CLI (v0.4.2) with a public track record (two completed pilots, 23 findings
— 21 PROVEN fired + 2 STRUCTURAL repo-verified); this grant funds
applying it to three more CKB-DAO-funded CKB/Fiber money products — each
shipped as one-command deterministic PoCs, minimal patches, and a
consent-based disclosure record — plus three net-new tool deliverables: a
standalone verify subcommand, a measured AI-cost reduction pass, and a
maintainer disclosure kit.
Type: developer security verification tooling (already built, MIT, single
static Go binary, zero runtime dependencies, CI green) plus a public body of
verified findings. Developers can also run ckb-whitehat locally as a
pre-push defensive security verification gate before shipping their own
CKB/Fiber apps. No changes to Fiber, CKB-VM, or any grantee’s codebase;
findings ship as PoCs + patches, applied only with the maintainer’s written
consent.
2. Team profile
Nghia Dang (GitHub: nghiadang391),
solo, all roles.
Contact:
Discord: nghia.dang.391
Email: nghia.dang.391@gmail.com
GitHub: https://github.com/nghiadang391
Nervos Talk: this account
Background: CKB ecosystem builder; author of the ckb-whitehat tool and
methodology (https://github.com/nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat,
MIT). Relevant public work, all verifiable in-repo:
Dular pilot (M-Pesa STK-push → RUSD on-ramp over Fiber; an approved
$2,000 Spark grant, M1 verified with 3 production 1-KES deposits): 9
findings — F1–F7 PROVEN (fired, including 1 CRITICAL) + F8–F9
STRUCTURAL (verified repo inventory / pre-release lockfile pin). F1
(“forged STK callback = free RUSD”) ends in a real CKB Pudge testnet trace
where a fabricated KES receipt moved RUSD between two of our own local FNN
nodes (tx hashes recorded in dular/FINDINGS.md, C4.1–C4.5). The F2
ledger double-spend race ships with a 3-line fix and a harness that fails
on unmodified source and passes on the fix.
tapfiber pilot (Fiber order/receipt library, vendored in-tree): 14
findings (F1–F14, all PROVEN/fired), one-command zero-dependency
offline PoC suite (node tapfiber/poc/attack.mjs).
The tool itself (v0.4.2): single static Go binary (zero runtime
dependencies — no Node/npm needed to install; drives local authenticated
claude, agy [Antigravity CLI], or codex CLIs in auto-detect order
claude → agy → codex, never asking for API keys), embedded methodology,
read-only AI-assisted init with per-command risk analysis and approval
(setup.json handoff), live responsive 2-column TUI with one-key human
checkpoint gates (triage / permission / publish), self-contained
local Docker CKB devnet (nervos/ckb:v0.210.0) + 2 peered Fiber
(nervos/fiber:0.10.1) nodes with pre-funded CKB & TEST_XUDT channels
(ckb-whitehat chain up|status|down), mainnet refusal guard + strict
post-run RPC hash verification, isolated Docker scratch Postgres
(127.0.0.1:5439), 5 embedded CKB/Fiber invariant packs, broad-allow +
strict high-risk denylist, polyglot stack support (Node, Rust/Cargo
ckb-testtool, Go, Python), install.sh + GitHub Releases (sha256-verified
self-update), and green CI.
Weekly sync: text updates in this thread, every Saturday at a fixed time
(UTC), with the week’s findings table and repro commands.
3. Project background
The grant cycle has produced a wave of CKB/Fiber money products —
stablecoin wallets, RUSD on-ramps, Fiber-based order/receipt systems, and
CKB-script apps. Where money moves, an unauthenticated callback, a ledger
double-spend race, or an unsafe config default is directly exploitable for
asset theft. Two lanes of verification already exist:
Protocol-core: the CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint and the
ckb-verify / spark-verify acceptance-check tool cover the shared chain
assets and the author’s own declared flows.
Author-side regression: a project re-running its own acceptance
commands on a devnet.
What is missing is the adversarial, community-owned middle lane: an outside
verifier testing the default code paths of funded apps — and giving builders
a reusable pre-push verification CLI they can run locally before shipping —
with deterministic evidence a maintainer can run and trust rather than a
report of opinions. The committee has shown it values concrete, verifiable
proof: the Dular approval turned on working multi-hop RUSD payment traces plus
a clear “How to Verify” section. This application funds that same shape — a
shipped tool (v0.4.2) with public evidence, applied to three new CKB/Fiber
targets.
4. Solution
For each target, ckb-whitehat executes a fixed, reproducible pipeline:
Read-only init & triage — ckb-whitehat init inspects the repo in
strictly read-only mode to map stack dependencies and host prerequisites
(with explicit per-command human approval for any target dependency install).
ckb-whitehat run then maps keygen/key storage, amount parsing (BigInt vs
Number), signing, vendor/network trust boundaries, balance/ledger
invariants, secrets-in-config, and on-chain interactions.
Named security invariant hypotheses — each names a code region, threat
class, and the money/safety invariant it violates (no double-credit,
non-negative balance under concurrency, callback authenticity, fail-closed
production defaults). Ranked and scoped to what is provable locally.
Deterministic PoCs — one replayable verification script per hypothesis:
unauthenticated-webhook test, concurrent DB race harness (against isolated
Docker scratch Postgres), config-matrix test, or boundary fuzz corpus. A
finding ships as PROVEN only when its script actually ran against
unmodified source and printed its captured FINDING <id> FIRED verdict.
On-chain evidence — for chain-interacting targets:
Local deterministic devnet (--chain): self-contained Docker CKB
devnet + 2 peered FNN v0.10.1 nodes with pre-funded CKB & TEST_XUDT
channels (zero faucet flakiness; every reported tx/payment hash is
automatically re-verified against local RPC by ckb-whitehat at the end
of run).
Public CKB Pudge testnet (when explorer-checkable public traces add
value): our own 2-node FNN stack, our own addresses, faucet assets —
impact confined strictly to our own addresses and local services. Mainnet
is hard-refused by the CLI.
Patch guidance — minimal defensive fix per finding; for races/config
bugs, a working fixed module plus the same harness re-run proving it fails
before and passes after.
Consent-based disclosure — private report to the maintainer, patch
window, publication only on written consent. The dated disclosure log ships
as a deliverable so the community sees the pipeline end to end.
How the AI cost enters: steps 1–3 use the local agent CLI (claude, agy,
or codex); LLM tokens for triage, PoC engineering, and report drafting are a
real, auditable cost item budgeted explicitly in §7 (capped at $150 across all
3 targets, with per-target session logs and token counts).
5. Technical approach
Stack: ckb-whitehat v0.4.2 static Go binary (go test -race green in
CI across Linux/macOS/Windows amd64/arm64) driving local claude, agy,
or codex CLIs, plus the target’s own runtime toolchain (polyglot support:
Node .mjs, Rust cargo test / ckb-testtool, Go, Python).
Local devnet & DB harness (already shipped in v0.3.x):
ckb-whitehat chain up boots an isolated Docker network (172.29.0.0/24)
with nervos/ckb:v0.210.0 (127.0.0.1:8114) + 2 peered
nervos/fiber:0.10.1 nodes (127.0.0.1:8227 / 8327), SHA-256-verified
Fiber contracts, pre-minted genesis CKB & TEST_XUDT, and pre-opened
ChannelReady CKB (1,000 CKB) + TEST_XUDT (100 TEST_XUDT) channels.
Five embedded reusable CKB/Fiber invariant packs materialized into every
workspace (chain-client.mjs, pack-payment-idempotency.mjs,
pack-hold-invoice-htlc.mjs, pack-udt-decimals.mjs,
pack-self-custody.mjs).
Auto-provisioned isolated Docker scratch Postgres (postgres:16-alpine on
127.0.0.1:5439, throwaway credentials) whenever a target uses Postgres.
Trust & safety boundaries:
Untrusted target isolation: --setting-sources user (Claude), no
--add-dir <target> (agy, blocking untrusted .agents/hooks.json),
project_doc_max_bytes=0 (Codex), hardened git clone (hooksPath=/dev/null,
fsmonitor=false, symlinks=false), and workspace-confined cwd.
Broad safe tool allowlist paired with a strict high-risk denylist blocking
rm -rf, git push, git reset --hard, sudo, curl, wget, ssh,
psql, env, live web fetches, MCP, and target-repo writes.
Mainnet refusal guard (VerifyMainnetSafe) checks CKB get_blockchain_info
and FNN chain_hash before any --chain run.
External third-party vendors (M-Pesa/Daraja, webhooks, external APIs) are
always mocked/stubbed locally; no live service is ever probed.
Hard parts:
Keeping every PoC deterministic and one-command reproducible against
unmodified source across heterogeneous stacks (JS/TS, Rust CKB-scripts,
Go).
Separating app-layer bugs from chain/FNN behavior in every recorded
on-chain state transition (linking upstream protocol issues rather than
claiming them as app findings).
Managing responsible disclosure timelines while keeping pre-consent
details private and still giving the committee an auditable dated log.
Language: English.
6. To-Do list (6 weeks)
The CLI (v0.4.2) and local CKB/Fiber devnet + scratch Postgres harness are
already built and proven on two pilots. The funded work is: (a) applying
ckb-whitehat to three new CKB-DAO-funded CKB/Fiber money products, and (b)
three net-new forward deliverables on the tool itself.
Week 1: D1 target selection posted in-thread (3 CKB-DAO-funded CKB/Fiber
projects from the active Spark/CKB registry, at least one a money product:
wallet / on-ramp / exchange / payment tool), with rationale and overlap check
against Sail-validation and author-side regression lanes. Verify local
devnet (ckb-whitehat chain up) + baseline green trace for Target 1 (and
optional Pudge testnet trace if public explorer verification applies).
Milestone: targets named and unchallenged for 7 days.
Week 2: Target 1, complete pack: offline findings + PoC suite + patch
guidance, local devnet / on-chain evidence (recorded hashes verified against
RPC), first private disclosure contact sent.
Milestone: Target 1 pack reproducible with one command per finding;
disclosure #1 sent.
Week 3: Target 2, complete pack + disclosure #2 sent.
Week 4: Target 3, complete pack + disclosure #3 sent.
Milestone: all three target packs merged to the repo, CI green.
Week 5: Net-new forward work (D6), three shippable PRs:
Standalone ckb-whitehat verify <FINDINGS.md> subcommand: unlike
v0.4.2’s in-run post-check, this standalone subcommand lets any
committee reviewer or maintainer re-audit an already published
FINDINGS.md with zero LLM calls — re-running its PoC suite and
re-verifying recorded tx/payment hashes against local devnet or Pudge
testnet RPC. Turns “How to Verify” into a single binary command.
Measured AI-cost reduction pass: establish a logged Week-1 token/cost
baseline per target, then cut total token spend via structured per-run
usage telemetry, prompt caching of the triage pass, tiered/smaller models
for mechanical checks, tighter gate-loop budgeting, and a hashed
known-issue catalog (recording deterministic (step, exit_code, error_class) hashes — never raw untrusted target output — mapped to
curated remedies so repeated environment failures short-circuit with zero
LLM turns and log recovered-known-issue <sig>). Target: ≥ 40% token
reduction vs. baseline while still firing every finding on re-run.
1-page quickstart + maintainer disclosure kit: a concise quickstart
for developers running ckb-whitehat pre-push on their own repo, plus
the exact public maintainer disclosure letter template and consent
checklist.
Cross-target SUMMARY.md (finding taxonomy, recurring foot-guns,
recommended community fixes) drafted alongside.
Week 6: Full regression re-run of every PoC against unmodified source;
secret-material sweep (confirming zero real provider keys, OTPs, phone PII,
or CKB hex keys in PoCs/reports); completion report with funds-usage vs. §7;
captioned 3-minute walkthrough demo of one full target run from init
through fired PoC and verified on-chain trace.
Milestone: final deliverable set live; ckb-whitehat verify green in CI.
7. Required funding & funding breakdown
Total: $950 USD, paid in CKB (within the standard $1,000 single-category
budget tier).
Technical vs. Community allocation: $850 technical (AI verification
compute, PoC/patch engineering, standalone verify subcommand, AI-cost
reduction pass) / $100 community (1-page developer quickstart, public
maintainer disclosure kit, weekly forum updates & maintainer disclosure

8. Deliverables + how to verify
A. Deliverables

rationale, overlap check against Sail-validation and author-side regression
lanes. Done when: posted and unchallenged for 7 days.
D2–D4 — Three target verification packs (Weeks 2–4): per-target
FINDINGS.md (severity-ranked PROVEN/STRUCTURAL/UNPROVEN findings,
captured PoC outputs, minimal patches, regression re-runs, verified on-chain
tx/payment hashes where applicable), reproducible poc/ suite, and
disclosure record. Done when: every PROVEN PoC reproduces with one
command against unmodified source and passes ckb-whitehat verify.
D5 — SUMMARY.md + dated disclosure log (Weeks 5–6): cross-target
finding taxonomy, recurring CKB/Fiber foot-guns, recommended fixes, and
dated record of every maintainer contact, patch-window status, and consent
state (public / consented-private / pending).
D6 — Three net-new forward PRs (Week 5):
Standalone ckb-whitehat verify <FINDINGS.md> subcommand — done when:

AI-cost reduction pass + hashed known-issue catalog — done when:

with identical findings fired, and a reproducing re-run logs
recovered-known-issue <sig>.
1-page developer quickstart + maintainer disclosure letter template —
done when: a developer can install and run ckb-whitehat on a fresh
target following only the 1-pager.
Completion report & 3-minute captioned demo (Week 6): funds usage vs.
§7 plus full run walkthrough video.
B. How to verify (no code review needed; low reviewer cost)
Environment & cost control:
Check 1 (offline pilot PoCs): Linux/macOS/Windows with Node 18+ only
— zero Docker, zero Postgres, zero network, ~5 seconds.
Check 2 (local CKB/Fiber devnet harness): Linux/macOS with Docker —
zero faucets, zero testnet keys, ~2 minutes.

0x72ed0d77…df27d3 from dular/poc/c4-record.json) or in any new D2–D4

9. Current state vs. funded work
Already exists (in nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat v0.4.2, uncosted by any grant):
Two completed pilots: Dular (F1–F7 PROVEN + F8–F9 STRUCTURAL +
on-chain C4.1–C4.5) and tapfiber (F1–F14, all PROVEN), with
reproducible PoCs and recorded traces.

AI-assisted init, responsive live TUI + checkpoint gates, self-contained

in-run completeness & RPC hash verification, broad-allow + strict denylist,
install.sh, sha256-verified update, and green CI.
Funded work (net-new under this $950 grant):
