Status: ready to run (tool shipped at v0.4.2). The repository
(https://github.com/nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat)
already exists under my GitHub account (nghiadang391) and holds two completed
pilots plus a working Go CLI release (v0.4.2, CI green). This application
funds the first systematic whitehat verification of three more CKB-DAO-funded
CKB/Fiber money products, plus three net-new forward deliverables on the tool
itself. Code for each new target lands in this repo week by week, with its
FINDINGS.md, its deterministic PoC suite, and its patch packs.

License: MIT.

Title: Spark Program | ckb-whitehat: deterministic whitehat verification of CKB/Fiber money products — AI-assisted triage, replayable PoCs, patches, consent-based disclosure

Category: DAOs & Funding → Spark Program (posted directly in the Spark sub-section per the 2026-07-19 forum update)

1. Project overview

  • Project name: ckb-whitehat
  • Repository: https://github.com/nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat (latest release: v0.4.2, MIT)
  • One-sentence summary: ckb-whitehat is a shipped community verification
    CLI (v0.4.2) with a public track record (two completed pilots, 23 findings
    — 21 PROVEN fired + 2 STRUCTURAL repo-verified); this grant funds
    applying it to three more CKB-DAO-funded CKB/Fiber money products — each
    shipped as one-command deterministic PoCs, minimal patches, and a
    consent-based disclosure record — plus three net-new tool deliverables: a
    standalone verify subcommand, a measured AI-cost reduction pass, and a
    maintainer disclosure kit.
  • Type: developer security verification tooling (already built, MIT, single
    static Go binary, zero runtime dependencies, CI green) plus a public body of
    verified findings. Developers can also run ckb-whitehat locally as a
    pre-push defensive security verification gate before shipping their own
    CKB/Fiber apps. No changes to Fiber, CKB-VM, or any grantee’s codebase;
    findings ship as PoCs + patches, applied only with the maintainer’s written
    consent.

2. Team profile

  • Nghia Dang (GitHub: nghiadang391),
    solo, all roles.
  • Contact:
    • Discord: nghia.dang.391
    • Email: nghia.dang.391@gmail.com
    • GitHub: https://github.com/nghiadang391
    • Nervos Talk: this account
  • Background: CKB ecosystem builder; author of the ckb-whitehat tool and
    methodology (https://github.com/nghiadang391/ckb-whitehat,
    MIT). Relevant public work, all verifiable in-repo:
    • Dular pilot (M-Pesa STK-push → RUSD on-ramp over Fiber; an approved
      $2,000 Spark grant, M1 verified with 3 production 1-KES deposits): 9
      findings       — F1–F7 PROVEN (fired, including 1 CRITICAL) + F8–F9
      STRUCTURAL       (verified repo inventory / pre-release lockfile pin). F1
      (“forged STK callback = free RUSD”) ends in a real CKB Pudge testnet trace
      where a fabricated KES receipt moved RUSD between two of our own local FNN
      nodes (tx hashes recorded in dular/FINDINGS.md, C4.1–C4.5). The F2
      ledger double-spend race ships with a 3-line fix and a harness that fails
      on unmodified source and passes on the fix.
    • tapfiber pilot (Fiber order/receipt library, vendored in-tree): 14
      findings (F1–F14, all PROVEN/fired)      , one-command zero-dependency
      offline PoC suite (node tapfiber/poc/attack.mjs).
    • The tool itself (v0.4.2): single static Go binary (zero runtime
      dependencies — no Node/npm needed to install; drives local authenticated
      claude, agy [Antigravity CLI], or codex CLIs in auto-detect order
      claude → agy → codex, never asking for API keys), embedded methodology,
      read-only AI-assisted init with per-command risk analysis and approval
      (setup.json handoff), live responsive 2-column TUI with one-key human
      checkpoint gates (triage / permission / publish), self-contained
      local Docker CKB devnet (nervos/ckb:v0.210.0) + 2 peered Fiber
      (nervos/fiber:0.10.1) nodes with pre-funded CKB & TEST_XUDT channels
      (ckb-whitehat chain up|status|down), mainnet refusal guard + strict
      post-run RPC hash verification, isolated Docker scratch Postgres
      (127.0.0.1:5439), 5 embedded CKB/Fiber invariant packs, broad-allow +
      strict high-risk denylist, polyglot stack support (Node, Rust/Cargo
      ckb-testtool, Go, Python), install.sh + GitHub Releases (sha256-verified
      self-update), and green CI.
  • Weekly sync: text updates in this thread, every Saturday at a fixed time
    (UTC), with the week’s findings table and repro commands.

3. Project background

The grant cycle has produced a wave of CKB/Fiber money products —
stablecoin wallets, RUSD on-ramps, Fiber-based order/receipt systems, and
CKB-script apps. Where money moves, an unauthenticated callback, a ledger
double-spend race, or an unsafe config default is directly exploitable for
asset theft. Two lanes of verification already exist:

  • Protocol-core: the CKB-VM Sail Validation Sprint and the
    ckb-verify / spark-verify acceptance-check tool cover the shared chain
    assets and the author’s own declared flows.
  • Author-side regression: a project re-running its own acceptance
    commands on a devnet.

What is missing is the adversarial, community-owned middle lane: an outside
verifier testing the default code paths of funded apps — and giving builders
a reusable pre-push verification CLI they can run locally before shipping —
with deterministic evidence a maintainer can run and trust rather than a
report of opinions. The committee has shown it values concrete, verifiable
proof: the Dular approval turned on working multi-hop RUSD payment traces plus
a clear “How to Verify” section. This application funds that same shape — a
shipped tool (v0.4.2) with public evidence, applied to three new CKB/Fiber
targets.

4. Solution

For each target, ckb-whitehat executes a fixed, reproducible pipeline:

  1. Read-only init & triage — ckb-whitehat init inspects the repo in
    strictly read-only mode to map stack dependencies and host prerequisites
    (with explicit per-command human approval for any target dependency install).
    ckb-whitehat run then maps keygen/key storage, amount parsing (BigInt vs
    Number), signing, vendor/network trust boundaries, balance/ledger
    invariants, secrets-in-config, and on-chain interactions.
  2. Named security invariant hypotheses — each names a code region, threat
    class, and the money/safety invariant it violates (no double-credit,
    non-negative balance under concurrency, callback authenticity, fail-closed
    production defaults). Ranked and scoped to what is provable locally.
  3. Deterministic PoCs — one replayable verification script per hypothesis:
    unauthenticated-webhook test, concurrent DB race harness (against isolated
    Docker scratch Postgres), config-matrix test, or boundary fuzz corpus. A
    finding ships as PROVEN only when its script actually ran against
    unmodified source and printed its captured FINDING <id> FIRED verdict.
  4. On-chain evidence — for chain-interacting targets:
    • Local deterministic devnet (--chain): self-contained Docker CKB
      devnet + 2 peered FNN v0.10.1 nodes with pre-funded CKB & TEST_XUDT
      channels (zero faucet flakiness; every reported tx/payment hash is
      automatically re-verified against local RPC by ckb-whitehat at the end
      of run).
    • Public CKB Pudge testnet (when explorer-checkable public traces add
      value):       our own 2-node FNN stack, our own addresses, faucet assets —
      impact confined strictly to our own addresses and local services. Mainnet
      is hard-refused by the CLI.
  5. Patch guidance — minimal defensive fix per finding; for races/config
    bugs, a working fixed module plus the same harness re-run proving it fails
    before and passes after.
  6. Consent-based disclosure — private report to the maintainer, patch
    window, publication only on written consent. The dated disclosure log ships
    as a deliverable so the community sees the pipeline end to end.

How the AI cost enters: steps 1–3 use the local agent CLI (claude, agy,
or codex); LLM tokens for triage, PoC engineering, and report drafting are a
real, auditable cost item budgeted explicitly in §7 (capped at $150 across all
3 targets, with per-target session logs and token counts).

5. Technical approach

  • Stack: ckb-whitehat v0.4.2 static Go binary (go test -race green in
    CI across Linux/macOS/Windows amd64/arm64) driving local claude, agy,
    or codex CLIs, plus the target’s own runtime toolchain (polyglot support:
    Node .mjs, Rust cargo test / ckb-testtool, Go, Python).
  • Local devnet & DB harness (already shipped in v0.3.x):
    • ckb-whitehat chain up boots an isolated Docker network (172.29.0.0/24)
      with nervos/ckb:v0.210.0 (127.0.0.1:8114) + 2 peered
      nervos/fiber:0.10.1 nodes (127.0.0.1:8227 / 8327), SHA-256-verified
      Fiber contracts, pre-minted genesis CKB & TEST_XUDT, and pre-opened
      ChannelReady CKB (1,000 CKB) + TEST_XUDT (100 TEST_XUDT) channels.
    • Five embedded reusable CKB/Fiber invariant packs materialized into every
      workspace (chain-client.mjs, pack-payment-idempotency.mjs,
      pack-hold-invoice-htlc.mjs, pack-udt-decimals.mjs,
      pack-self-custody.mjs).
    • Auto-provisioned isolated Docker scratch Postgres (postgres:16-alpine on
      127.0.0.1:5439, throwaway credentials) whenever a target uses Postgres.
  • Trust & safety boundaries:
    • Untrusted target isolation: --setting-sources user (Claude), no
      --add-dir <target> (agy, blocking untrusted .agents/hooks.json),
      project_doc_max_bytes=0 (Codex), hardened git clone (hooksPath=/dev/null,
      fsmonitor=false, symlinks=false), and workspace-confined cwd.
    • Broad safe tool allowlist paired with a strict high-risk denylist blocking
      rm -rf, git push, git reset --hard, sudo, curl, wget, ssh,
      psql, env, live web fetches, MCP, and target-repo writes.
    • Mainnet refusal guard (VerifyMainnetSafe) checks CKB get_blockchain_info
      and FNN chain_hash before any --chain run.
    • External third-party vendors (M-Pesa/Daraja, webhooks, external APIs) are
      always mocked/stubbed locally; no live service is ever probed.
  • Hard parts:
    • Keeping every PoC deterministic and one-command reproducible against
      unmodified source across heterogeneous stacks (JS/TS, Rust CKB-scripts,
      Go).
    • Separating app-layer bugs from chain/FNN behavior in every recorded
      on-chain state transition (linking upstream protocol issues rather than
      claiming them as app findings).

    3. 1-page quickstart + maintainer disclosure kit: a concise quickstart

CellCat is a fully on-chain genetic cat game built on CKB. The gameplay is simple: Adopt → Breed to produce eggs → Wait for block-based hatching → List for sale or burn cats.
Why CKB?
Real floor value for every cat: Each cat is represented by a real Cell. Feeding a cat means depositing CKB into its Cell. If you no longer want to play, you can simply “burn” the cat and recover all the CKB stored in its Cell back to your wallet.
No images stored on-chain; genetics are computed on-chain: Each cat stores only 32 bytes of DNA (dominant + recessive genes). Breeding first produces an egg. Smart contract testing

All tests are passing.
Mobile-friendly web application
The cattery, breeding system, marketplace, postcard generation, and basic social interactions are all playable on the local Devnet.

Week 4:
Integrate JoyID on Testnet.
Deliver the source code and a recorded demonstration.
